title: Daily activities
title_target: まいにち なにを しますか — Mainichi nani o shimasu ka
goal: Talk about what you do every day: ます-form verbs with their objects, where the activity happens, what you use, and who you're with.
bekal: using を to mark the object
using で for the place of an activity and for tools
using へ / に for direction
using と to say who you're with
describing a whole day in Japanese

dialogs.title: 会話 1 — What's your day like?
dialogs.intro: Tanaka asks about Ani's routine. Notice how a single sentence can hold time, place, object and verb all at once — and always in that order.

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [アニさんは|Ani-san wa] [まいにち|mainichi] [なにを|nani o] [しますか|shimasu ka]。
lines.id: Ani, what do you do every day?

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [あさ|Asa] [がっこうで|gakkō de] [にほんごを|Nihongo o] [べんきょうします|benkyō shimasu]。
lines.id: In the morning I study Japanese at school.

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [ごごは|Gogo wa]？
lines.id: And in the afternoon?

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [ごごは|Gogo wa] [としょかんで|toshokan de] [ほんを|hon o] [よみます|yomimasu]。
lines.id: In the afternoon I read books at the library.
lines.literal: afternoon — as-for — library — at — book — [object] — read.

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [ひとりで|Hitori de] [いきますか|ikimasu ka]。
lines.id: Do you go alone?

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [いいえ|Iie]、[ともだちと|tomodachi to] [いきます|ikimasu]。[ときどき|Tokidoki] [カフェで|kafe de] [コーヒーを|kōhī o] [のみます|nomimasu]。
lines.id: No, I go with a friend. Sometimes we have coffee at a café.
lines.literal: no, friend — with — go. sometimes — café — at — coffee — [object] — drink.

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [うちへは|Uchi e wa] [なんじに|nanji ni] [かえりますか|kaerimasu ka]。
lines.id: What time do you get home?
lines.literal: home — to — as-for — what-o'clock — at — return — [question].

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [ろくじごろ|Roku-ji goro] [かえります|kaerimasu]。[でんしゃで|Densha de] [かえります|kaerimasu]。
lines.id: Around six. I go home by train.
lines.literal: six-o'clock — around — return. train — by — return.

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [よるは|Yoru wa] [なにを|nani o] [しますか|shimasu ka]。
lines.id: What do you do in the evening?

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [ばんごはんを|Bangohan o] [つくります|tsukurimasu]。[それから|Sorekara] [テレビを|terebi o] [みます|mimasu]。
lines.id: I cook dinner. After that I watch TV.

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [まいにち|Mainichi] [いそがしいですね|isogashii desu ne]。
lines.id: You're busy every day, aren't you?

notes: **Japanese word order is far looser than you'd expect** — except for one thing: **the verb always comes last**. Otherwise the most natural order is: who は — when — where で — what を — verb.
**します = do**, the most versatile verb of all. Combined with nouns it forms hundreds of new verbs: べんきょう**します** (study), しごと**します** (work), そうじ**します** (clean), でんわ**します** (phone).
**ごろ vs ぐらい.** ごろ is for **points in time** (6じごろ = around 6 o'clock), ぐらい for **amounts and durations** (5ふんぐらい = about 5 minutes). Swapping them sounds wrong to Japanese ears right away.
**ひとりで = alone**, with で. Its counterpart ともだち**と** = with a friend, uses と. Two different particles for two related ideas.
**それから = after that**, used to chain activities in sequence. Its relatives: そして (and then), でも (but), だから (so).
**うちへは — two stacked particles.** へ marks direction, は makes it the topic. This is perfectly normal and used for contrast: “as for getting home, what time?”

grammars.title: [を|o] and [で|de] — the two most often confused particles
body: **[を|o]** marks the **object**: what the action is done to. **[で|de]** marks the **place of an activity** or a **tool/means**. Both often appear in one sentence, and the order is almost always place first, object second.

head: Sentence
Meaning
What's marked
rows: [としょかんで|Toshokan de] [よみます|yomimasu]。
[としょかんで|Toshokan de] [ほんを|hon o] [よみます|yomimasu]。
I read a book at the library.
[にほんごで|Nihongo de] [はなします|hanashimasu]。
[ともだちと|Tomodachi to] [はなします|hanashimasu]。

after: ⚠️ **[で|de] (place of activity) vs [に|ni] (place of existence).** Compare: [きょうしつ|kyōshitsu]**[に|ni]** [います|imasu] (to be **in** the classroom — Unit 5) and [きょうしつ|kyōshitsu]**[で|de]** [べんきょうします|benkyō shimasu] (to study **in** the classroom). If something is being done, use [で|de]. If you're only saying something is there, use [に|ni]. This is the most important particle distinction at A1.
⚠️ **[を|o] is written with the kana [を|o], not [お|o].** This kana is used only as a particle and never appears inside words.

grammars.title: [へ|e] and [に|ni] for direction
body: With verbs of motion — [いきます|ikimasu] (go), [きます|kimasu] (come), [かえります|kaerimasu] (go home) — the destination is marked with **[へ|e]** or **[に|ni]**. The two are almost interchangeable.
The difference is slight: **[へ|e]** stresses the **direction**, **[に|ni]** the **point of arrival**. In everyday use, either is fine.
⚠️ **The particle [へ|e] is read *e*, not *he*.** This is the second exception after [は|wa], which is read *wa*.

head: Sentence
Meaning
rows: [どこへ|Doko e] [いきますか|ikimasu ka]。
[でんしゃで|Densha de] [えきへ|eki e] [いきます|ikimasu]。
I go to the station by train.

after: **The full chain:** [まいにち|Mainichi] [でんしゃで|densha de] [がっこうへ|gakkō e] [いきます|ikimasu]。 — when, by what, where to, verb. This order sounds the most natural.

dialogs.title: 会話 2 — The weekend
dialogs.intro: Budi talks about his weekend plans. Watch for the frequency adverbs that appear in several lines.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [ブディさんは|Budi-san wa] [しゅうまつ|shūmatsu] [なにを|nani o] [しますか|shimasu ka]。
lines.id: Budi, what do you do on weekends?

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: [どようびは|Doyōbi wa] [うちで|uchi de] [やすみます|yasumimasu]。[にちようびは|Nichiyōbi wa] [こうえんで|kōen de] [サッカーを|sakkā o] [します|shimasu]。
lines.id: On Saturday I rest at home. On Sunday I play soccer in the park.
lines.literal: Saturday — as-for — home — at — rest. Sunday — as-for — park — at — soccer — [object] — do.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [よく|Yoku] [サッカーを|sakkā o] [しますか|shimasu ka]。
lines.id: Do you play soccer often?

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: [まいしゅう|Maishū] [します|shimasu]。[インドネシアじんの|Indoneshia-jin no] [ともだちと|tomodachi to] [します|shimasu]。
lines.id: Every week. I play with my Indonesian friends.
lines.literal: every-week — do. Indonesia-person — 's — friend — with — do.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [おもしろそうですね|Omoshirosō desu ne]。[わたしは|Watashi wa] [スポーツを|supōtsu o] [あまり|amari] [しません|shimasen]。
lines.id: Sounds fun. I don't do much sport.
lines.literal: interesting-looking — is — right. I — as-for — sport — [object] — not-much — don't-do.

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: [じゃあ|Jā]、[なにを|nani o] [しますか|shimasu ka]。
lines.id: So what do you do?

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [おんがくを|Ongaku o] [ききます|kikimasu]。[それから|Sorekara] [えいがを|eiga o] [みます|mimasu]。
lines.id: I listen to music. And I watch movies.

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: [どこで|Doko de] [えいがを|eiga o] [みますか|mimasu ka]。
lines.id: Where do you watch them?

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [うちで|Uchi de] [みます|mimasu]。[えいがかんへは|Eigakan e wa] [ぜんぜん|zenzen] [いきません|ikimasen]。
lines.id: At home. I never go to the movie theater.
lines.literal: home — at — watch. movie-theater — to — as-for — at-all — don't-go.

lines.speaker: ブディ:
lines.text: [こんどの|Kondo no] [にちようび|nichiyōbi]、[いっしょに|issho ni] [いきませんか|ikimasen ka]。
lines.id: Want to go together next Sunday?

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [いいですね|Ii desu ne]。[いきましょう|Ikimashō]。
lines.id: Sounds good. Let's go.

notes: **あまり and ぜんぜん always pair with a negative verb.** あまり しません = don't do much. ぜんぜん いきません = never go at all. Using them with a positive verb is a grammar error, not just a matter of style.
**よく has two meanings:** “often” (よくいきます) and “well” (よくわかりました). Context tells them apart, and both are very common.
**いっしょに = together**, unlike と, which names **who**. You can use both at once: ともだちと いっしょに いきます.
**～ませんか = a gentle invitation**, literally “won't you ～?”. In Japanese, inviting with a negative sounds more polite than with a positive — it leaves room to say no. Fully covered in Unit 9.
**こんどの = the coming / next.** こんどのにちようび = next Sunday. The word is slippery: it can mean “this time” or “next time” depending on context.
**おもしろそう = sounds interesting.** The ending ～そう expresses an impression from the outside. Not required at this level, but too useful not to recognize.

grammars.title: Frequency adverbs
body: These words go **before the verb**, and three of them require a negative verb. The right-hand column is a rule you can't break.
after: **A matched pair:** [よく|Yoku] [コーヒーを|kōhī o] [のみます|nomimasu]。 / [あまり|Amari] [コーヒーを|kōhī o] [のみません|nomimasen]。 — two sentences where the verb form has to change too.

grammars.title: Your first thirty verbs
body: These verbs cover most everyday conversation. All are written in the [ます|masu] form. Learn them together with their objects — the brain remembers phrases far better than single words.

head: Verb
Meaning
Example phrase
rows: [にほんごを|Nihongo o] [はなします|hanashimasu]
[りょうりを|ryōri o] [つくります|tsukurimasu]
[にほんごを|Nihongo o] [べんきょうします|benkyō shimasu]

head: Verb
Meaning
Example phrase
rows: [はたらきます|hatarakimasu] 働きます
[かいしゃで|kaisha de] [はたらきます|hatarakimasu]
[わかります|wakarimasu] 分かります
[にほんごが|Nihongo ga] [わかります|wakarimasu]

after: ⚠️ **Two verbs with unexpected particles:** [ともだち|tomodachi]**[に|ni]** [あいます|aimasu] (meet a friend — [に|ni], not [と|to] or [を|o]) and [にほんご|nihongo]**[が|ga]** [わかります|wakarimasu] (understand Japanese — [が|ga], not [を|o]). There are a dozen or so verbs like this; learn them with their particles from day one.

blocks.text: Japanese sentences grow by adding information **in front of** the verb, not after it. Watch a short sentence expand without a single part needing to change:

head: Step
Sentence
Meaning
rows: [しょくどうで|Shokudō de] [ごはんを|gohan o] [たべます|tabemasu]。
I eat a meal in the cafeteria.
[じゅうにじに|Jūni-ji ni] [しょくどうで|shokudō de] [ごはんを|gohan o] [たべます|tabemasu]。
I eat a meal in the cafeteria at 12.
[まいにち|Mainichi] [じゅうにじに|jūni-ji ni] [しょくどうで|shokudō de] [ごはんを|gohan o] [たべます|tabemasu]。
Every day I eat a meal in the cafeteria at 12.
[ともだちと|Tomodachi to] [まいにち|mainichi] [じゅうにじに|jūni-ji ni] [しょくどうで|shokudō de] [ごはんを|gohan o] [たべます|tabemasu]。
Every day at 12 I eat a meal in the cafeteria with a friend.

blocks.title: The most natural order
items: **Who は — When — With whom と — Where で — By what で — What を — Verb**
This order isn't a fixed rule; Japanese speakers shift things around for emphasis. But if you follow it, your sentences will never sound odd.
Only one thing is **fixed**: the verb at the end. That never moves.

blocks.text: Every means of transport takes the particle **で**, except walking, which uses the special form あるいて.

head: Japanese
Meaning
Example
rows: [ちかてつで|chikatetsu de] [かえります|kaerimasu]
[じてんしゃで|jitensha de] [いきます|ikimasu]
[タクシーで|takushī de] [かえります|kaerimasu]
⚠️ [あるいて|aruite] [いきます|ikimasu] — no で

blocks.text: **Trains in Japan.** JR is the national network; the rest belong to private companies and cities. IC cards (Suica, PASMO, ICOCA) work almost everywhere in the country and can also pay at convenience stores — this one card saves a lot of conversations at the ticket counter.
